newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 8.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- BAT SEEKS PARTNER AFTER CU TALKS FAIL

Despite the failure of talks with Commercial Union Plc, B.A.T Industries is looking for a merger partner for its financial services division. The group is keen to merge its financial arm, which owns the Eagle Star and Allied Dunbar insurance businesses in Britain, Farmers in the US and Threadneedle Asset Management with a major financial operator.
-- GOLDIE BARRED FOR FIVE YEARS

Former managing director of the collapsed British and Commonwealth, Peter Goldie, has been disqualified, by the High Court, from being a company director or being involved in any management capacity for five years. The Deputy Registrar said he had taken into consideration the time lapse since the collapse and the fact that Goldie had not made any personal gain and was out of the business environment.
-- NIKE SIGNS UP BRAZIL FOR $400 MILLION

The global sportswear group Nike has signed a $400 million contract with the Brazilian football team, the world's biggest sports sponsorship deal. The contract gives Nike the right to arrange a series of international soccer fixtures with Brazil as part of the group's new drive into sports promotion.
-- GREENALLS PUTS FRUIT MACHINES UP FOR SALE

The pub and restaurant group Greenalls has put its fruit machine distribution business, Stretton Leisure, up for sale as part of a 150 million stg disposal programme designed to focus the group on its core operations. The business operates 40,000 machines and makes profits of about five million stg a year. Greenalls hopes to raise 40 million stg from the sale and a management buy-out is thought likely.
-- BOOTS PRESCRIBES A LOYALTY CARD

Boots is planning to launch a loyalty card next year in an effort to boost sales and learn more about its customers. The group is carrying out trials of a smart card which would give savings of five percent and carry all the user's prescription details. Boots will produce the first smart card in general use in Britain. SUNDAY TIMES
-- DTI CLOSE TO CENTRE OF CITY INSIDER DEALING RING

Investigators from the DTI have identified two Monaco- resident British financiers who are at the centre of a City insider dealing ring. The two men are thought to form the offshore connection to a London-based ring that has been under investigation for five years.
-- BRITISH GAS PLANS TO SELL TROPHY FIELD

British Gas is likely to sell Britain's biggest gas field, Morecombe Bay, as it tries to resolve its row with North Sea gas producers over take-or-pay contracts worth tens of million of pounds. The field could be sold to a single purchaser or broken up into smaller parcels to overcome the crisis, in which British Gas has incurred liabilities of two billion stg.
-- 180 MILLION STG LIKELY FOR BA SLOTS

The world's most profitable airline, British Airways, is set for a 180 million stg windfall from the sale of the first batch of take-off and landing slots that it has to sell to satisfy the conditions imposed by the government on its alliance with American Airlines. BA would also generate extra revenue from the remaining 70 slots that the Office of Fair Trading indicated could be released in two batches in 1998.
-- SHELL SHINES IN ADDING VALUE FOR SHAREHOLDERS

Findings from a Sunday Times survey, carried out with the American consultancy Stern Stewart, which calculated the Market Value Added for the UK's top companies, have revealed that Shell, Glaxo Wellcome and SmithKline Beecham have delivered more shareholder value than any other UK quoted companies. British Steel, Hanson and Trafalgar House trail the field in failing to make good returns for investors on the capital entrusted to them.
-- GRANDMET'S SHIPPAMS PASTE TO GO

Grand Metropolitan, the Smirnoff vodka to Burger King giant, is close to selling its Shippams Paste brand as part of a 150 million stg worth of disposals to be concluded by the new year. Shippams will be sold to a trade buyer for less than 20 million stg. Businesses worth another 100 million stg will be sold over the next month, completing a 300 million stg disposal programme at Pillsbury.
THE OBSERVER
-- HESELTINE BREAKFAST CLUB PLAN FLOPS

A scheme, which was backed by the Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine and spearheaded by British Airways chairman and president of CBI, Sir Colin Marshall, has flopped. The plan was to form a lobby group to promote the privatised industries. Nearly all of the UK's privatised companies will boycott the inaugural meeting though fear that the campaign would be seen as too much of a political statement in the run-up to a general election.
-- STRONG POUND ADDS 45 MILLION STG TO LLOYDS BILLS

Thousands of hard-hit Lloyds Names are to face an additional 45 million stg bill because of currency fluctuations since the rescue package was calculated. Lloyd's is demanding up to six percent more from Names to reflect the recent surge in the value of the pound against the dollar. The increase will affect all 12,000 Names who still participate in the market and those who have run up losses since 1992.
-- EU TO GET TOUGH WITH BA ALLIANCE

British Airways could be facing tough restrictions from the EU over its proposed alliance with American Airlines, tougher than those put forward by the UK Government. The EC believes the worldwide partnership raises serious competition issues. The Commission's transport and competition directorates are examining the deal and could make a decision by February.
-- LANG DEFENDS POSITION ON LABOUR STANDARDS AS 'NOT STONY- HEARTED'

Ian Lang, the trade secretary, has defended the Government's refusal to force other countries to meet minimum labour standards as a condition of trade. He said that it did not reflect a 'stony-hearted' indifference to the plight of those trapped in bonded labour. He says that sanctions would throw the poor out of work altogether. INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- EMI SEEKS MERGER WITH MCA

The music group EMI has approached Seagram about merging all or part of its business with the latter's MCA Music division. The deal would mean that Seagram assumed overall control with key roles for both Sir Colin Southgate, EMI's chairman, and Jim Fifield, chief executive. Any agreed deal would value EMI at 6.5 billion stg or more.
-- POUND IN FOR MORE STRIFE

Turmoil in the foreign exchanges is to come this week after comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan that "irrational exuberance" in the markets could lead to further turmoil for the dollar, and sterling is in disarray after Tory party strife. Stock markets tumbled worldwide on Friday, wiping 20 billion stg of the value of UK shares.
-- TV BOSSES 'BLEW THEIR CHANCE TO THWART MURDOCH'

Stephen Barden, a former top executive of BSkyB has attacked British television industry chiefs for missing opportunities to co-operate to combat the growing dominance of Rupert Murdoch as satellite broadcaster in the digital television revolution. He claims the BBC, ITV and Channel Four passed up the chance 18 months ago to set up a united front to make digital terrestrial TV a competitor to BSkyB.
-- CONRAN PLANS RIVAL TO CAFE ROUGE

In an attempt to rival Cafe Rouge, Sir Terence Conran will launch a chain of affordable French-style eateries. He may seek a market quote to raise funds. The chain will be called Zinc Bar and Grill and will open its first outlet in the West End of London next year.
-- BID DISPUTE HEATS UP AT KENWOOD

Kenwood is denying claims that the electrical appliance maker Pifco, which takes in the Salton and Russel Hobbs brands, has made a former offer for the group. Michael Webber, Pifco chairman, claims he had written to Kenwood on July 5 with a formal offer. Pifco hopes to put the two independent appliance makers together to create a more powerful international group.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- BARCLAYS TO BANK A NEW BRITANNIA

Barclay's Bank is considering leading a consortium to fund an 80 million stg replacement for the Royal Yacht Britannia. The new vessel would be used to promote British exports abroad, and will contain apartments exclusively for the Royal Family's use. The proposal was put forward by the British Exporters Association.
-- ALLIANCE GETS GO-AHEAD

Members of the Alliance and Leicester building society have voted in favour of a 2.5 billion stg conversion to a bank. Polls conducted by the society suggest that savers and borrowers have backed the conversion. However, the Alliance and Leicester Action Group, will accuse the society of offering an unfair windfall scheme.
-- TROUBLE IN STORE OVER SELL-OFF PLAN

Splits are emerging within the board of stores group Sears over the sale of the mail order division Freemans. Some directors are believed to be insisting on a price close to the 470 million stg Sears paid in 1988. Potential buyers, including Littlewoods and Otto, are thought to value Freemans at less than 400 million stg.
-- ABBEY REBUFFS THE MAN FROM PRU

Abbey National is fending off advances from Prudential over a possible merger. Peter Birch, chief executive at Abbey, has told his big institutional shareholders that he has no intention of agreeing to a deal. The rumours are thought to have been circulated in the market to test Abbey's response to a proposal from Peter Davis, Prudential's chief executive.
-- CARTEL LOSSES ITS CAP

The Association of Policy Market Makers, a cartel of traders in second-hand endowment policies has lost its battle with business watchdogs. It pledged to end a cap on commission to financial advisors who buy or sell endowment policies for clients, however, the Office of Fair Trading demanded they drop a clause barring members from paying more than three percent commission to advisors.
